[PAPER_0040, relevance_score=0.346] In these experiments, rewards were presented as "gifts. Experiment 2 further manipulated reward contingency using traditional monetary rewards to test if the findings from Experiment 1 could be replicated.

Based on our hypothesis, we expected Experiments 1 and 2 to show that task-switch costs can be reduced after random rewards.

Indeed, Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrated the anticipated reduction in switch costs following random rewards; however, this reduction was accompanied by significant post-reward slowing on both switch and repeat trials.

q2: We hypothesize that switch costs (the difference in response time on task switch trials vs. task repeat trials, a common index of cognitive flexibility) will be decreased in the performance noncontingent reward phase as compared to the performance contingent reward phase.

Response time data will be subjected to a 2 (reward: trial follows reward, trial does not follow reward) x 2 (transition type: switch, repeat) x 2 (phase: contingent, noncontingent) repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) using the rstatix package (Kassambara, 2020) in R (R Core Team, 2019). [PREREG_0013, relevance_score=0.265] q22: We will also conduct a causal mediation analysis using the mediation R package (Tingley et al., 2014) to determine whether the relationship between rewards (particularly noncontingent ones) and switch costs is mediated by changes in affect. [PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.333] Design and Procedure

Participants alternated between size and animacy categorization tasks with a 50% chance of being cued by the frame color to perform either task. Instead of negative rewards, positive monetary rewards were offered to participants. Accordingly, the counter in the bottom right of the screen now started at 0 and increased by 5 cents each time a reward was presented. Unlike Experiment 1 with only one random reward condition, Experiment 2 manipulated reward contingency: Rewards were given out either contingent or not contingent on performance.

[PAPER_0062, relevance_score=0.303] However, we overestimated the degree of performance improvement with time-on-task, and the final reward rate was only 26% (SD = 13).

The two conditions were blocked, and the order was counterbalanced across participants. Participants were informed about the upcoming contingency at the beginning of each condition-"During this portion of the experiment, you will randomly be given money. The computer has randomly selected when to give this money" or "During this portion of the experiment, you will earn money based on your performance. You can earn money for responding fast and accurately.
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 2 manipulated reward contingency, preceding-trial reward, and task transition within participants. Phase order was counterbalanced, and task cues had a 50% probability for each task [PAPER_0053] [PAPER_0054] [PAPER_0062] [PAPER_0070].

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.285] Analysis

To determine whether reward contingency determines the aftereffect of reward on switch costs, median RT and ER were separately subjected to a 2 (reward contingency: contingent, random) × 2 (n - 1 trial outcome: reward, nothing) × 2 (transition: switch, repeat) repeated measure ANOVA. Note that the preregistration protocol erroneously stated the use of post hoc ANOVAs to follow up on the critical three-way interactions. Instead, we examined the pattern and conducted directional paired t tests to identify the differences driving the interaction.

[PAPER_0090, relevance_score=0.317] In this ANOVA context, if the observed effect of rewards on switch costs (reaction times) were due to posterror adaptive processes, the three-way interaction involving n - 1 trial accuracy, n - 1 trial outcome, and transition would be significant. To help detect this three-way interaction, we pooled data from all four experiments. However, due to generally high performance in this paradigm, not all participants had enough trials in each condition.

The second approach involves further excluding trials following errors to minimize the influence of posterror adaptive processes on the observed random rewards effect.
